title: Impact of a CSS quantum error correction code in underwater quantum key distribution
authors: Juliette Florin, Nicolas Le Josse, Arnaud Coatanhay, Gilles Burel
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables secure underwater communications essential for maritime infrastructure. Underwater optical channels introduce substantial photon loss (erasures) and ambient noise that degrade QKD performance. This paper investigates whether two four-qubit Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error correction codes (QECC) mitigate these impairments in vertical underwater communication BB84 QKD protocol. After developing a comprehensive stochastic channel model incorporating photon loss, geometric spreading, and solar noise, we assess the viability of QECC through the analytical study of the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and the secure key rate (SKR) with and without security depending on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) validated against Monte Carlo simulations. The standard four-qubit CSS code achieves a 3 dB SNR gain at the QBER 11% security threshold; the discard code variant achieves 4.5 dB. However, QECC includes an encoding overhead that reduces the SKR. We demonstrate a crucial relationship between the SKR and the probability of arrival of the sent photon. Analysis shows that QECC is beneficial exclusively in marginal SNR regimes; at high SNR, raw BB84 dominates. For an ocean Type III Jerlov water scenario with sunlight coming from the sun located at the top of the atmosphere, we identify operational depth-range windows where QECC enables communication otherwise infeasible. This analysis establishes that error correction deployment must be scenario-dependent: extend operational range at the cost of throughput when SNR is marginal, or prioritize key generation rates at high SNR.
summary: This paper analyzes the feasibility of using Quantum Error Correction Codes (QECC) to secure quantum key distribution in noisy underwater channels. By modeling photon loss and ambient noise, the authors show that while QECC extends the operational range at low SNR, its overhead makes raw BB84 superior when the signal quality is high. The deployment strategy must therefore be highly dependent on the local SNR conditions.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether Quantum Error Correction Codes (QECC) can mitigate performance degradation in Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) when transmitting underwater due to photon loss and ambient noise.
main_result: QECC is beneficial only in marginal Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) regimes, enabling communication in depth ranges otherwise infeasible, but raw BB84 dominates at high SNR due to encoding overhead.
method: The authors developed a stochastic channel model incorporating photon loss, geometric spreading, and solar noise, analyzing the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) and Secure Key Rate (SKR) analytically and via Monte Carlo simulations.
model_or_system: The system models vertical underwater quantum communication using the BB84 protocol. The channel is treated as a CPTP map incorporating signal loss, vacuum events, and noise photon arrivals, analyzed using 4-qubit CSS stabilizer codes.
key_observables: Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) and Secure Key Rate (SKR).
important_parameters: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), QBER threshold (11% for security), and the specific type of error correction code used (standard vs. discard).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a homogeneous water medium, negligible scattering noise, and that the dominant error mechanism is photon loss (erasure channel).
figures_summary: Figures compare QBER and SKR vs. SNR for raw BB84, standard QECC, and discard QECC, demonstrating the performance trade-offs across different SNR regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, develops the stochastic channel and performance metrics (QBER, SKR), analyzes the benefits and overhead of QECC, and concludes with scenario-dependent deployment guidelines.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, applied study of how quantum error correction techniques must be tailored to the specific noise characteristics of a complex physical channel (underwater optics) to maintain secure communication.
